video_title: Christopher Merrill on Building $110B Harrison Street
transcript: [music] [music] >> Tarper, great to see you. >> Great to be here. >> Why don't you take me back to whatever early influences [music] in your life, if you look back, had something to do with you becoming an investor? >> You know, it's interesting. I, you know, when I was when I was a teenager, um there was a gentleman in town I'm I'm from the suburbs of Chicago that had a real estate firm uh called Heitman. Um and for me, you know, I would overhear his conversations and hear him talk about the business. And I remember when I was 16, 17, I would say, you know, boy, I'd love to work for you someday. And he basically said, look at after your first year college, uh we offer summer internships. And it was with that, you know, after my freshman year college, I I I did a summer internship and did one every summer during college with with with the firm and it was sort of, you know, enhanced my love of real estate and uh kind of gave me the bug and that's how it all got started. >> Do you remember what it was about real estate that first got you interested? >> You know, for me, what what I've always loved about the business is the the ability to kind of almost touch and feel like you can see the value, you can point to the asset. Um Chicago is a a really cool architectural city and so it was a lot of fun just sort of seeing these assets and these buildings and the fact that, you know, you could sort of wrap your arms around what the value of that asset is. And so for me, I was just always very interested in the valuation of these different properties. And so that's sort of something I always liked about the business. >> So did you got started, where did that career path take you in the initial years? >> So it's interesting. So, you know, for for one summer I was in the um property management leasing, so I really cut my teeth learning how to sort of manage an asset. Uh then I was in a construction department uh the second summer and the final summer I was in the acquisitions, the transactions group uh and really just learning to underwrite different assets, was ultimately hired into that group, started a week after my college graduation in the Acquisitions Group. Did that for a while, and then the former chairman of the company was looking for someone to almost be his assistant as he was looking at more opportunistic investments with his personal capital, some of the partners' capital. And I kind of just raised my hand and said, hey, can I be that guy? And so I was the assistant to the chairman of the board and was working on some some very interesting transactions. We we bought 2,000 acres of land out at Snowmass. We did a non-airport industrial company. So it was definitely out of the box investing. And for me, it just kept pushing me and and ultimately formed sort of a a corporate development group within the firm and that then led to the the next steps where I ended up going to Europe as well. >> What did you find in Europe? >> So, you know, the you know, you you look back on some of the the the fork in the road kind of situations. I was working on sort of the non-traditional assets at the firm, and there was a developer in town that had began exploring Eastern Europe. And this is in sort of the mid-90s. The wall had come down. Mid-90s, this this developer had gone overseas and basically said, hey, would you like to go on a a 10-day trip around Central and Eastern Europe? I want to show you what's going on. And so I sort of got the approval to do that, went and spent time in, you know, Warsaw and Prague and Budapest and then went to Kiev and St. Petersburg. And it was fascinating. I had never really been outside the country much, let alone to these parts of the world. But it was for me really eye-opening because I I was spending a lot of time in in cities like Warsaw and then Prague and Budapest and basically recognizing that the wall had come down. There's 3 to 400 million people that now had a taste of capitalism and wanted goods and services. Every consumer goods company wanted to be there. That meant every law firm, every marketing firm was going to be there, consulting firms. But there was no office space, there was no industrial buildings, there was no really any decent residential. Everybody was working out of old hotels. So I basically said, boy, wouldn't this be a great opportunity to invest in real estate in this market? And I ended up writing, I always say a a Jerry Maguire memo and when I say that the younger folks don't really know that in the firm, but I sort of wrote this memo to the board that I cringe when I read it today, but basically saying, hey, can I move to London and be the first, you know, we've never really the firm had never really done any business outside the US. Can I move to London and can I try and develop a business in Central Europe? You know, these were countries that were part of the part of NATO, weren't part of the European Union, but they weren't going back. And again, to the the firm's credit, the former chairman of the time said said go for it. I have a friend in London, go go do it. And I moved over there and started this journey of investing in Central Europe in the late 90s. >> What was different about tackling a nascent opportunity from a more traditional real estate where you're just looking at existing markets and supply and demand trends? >> You know, for me it was just trying to different you trying to I I guess trying to be different, right? And for me, what was really exciting about this opportunity is it was a bunch of foreigners in these markets. So if you think about it, we were when I was in Central Europe, it was, you know, British and French and American developers and Austrian and German banks. And it was a lot of very entrepreneurial people that saw this opportunity to to invest in these countries. And so what was different about it, it was a lot of you had to do a lot of leg work yourself. You know, it wasn't I couldn't go get a Jones Lang LaSalle office market study for Warsaw at the time. And so a lot of it was, you know, put your running shoes on and pad a paper and really go understand where the office markets are going to develop and you know, meeting a lot of new folks. So for me, it was a lot of you You there was so much opaqueness with the market, you had to really start extrapolating things. And so, for instance, it was okay, in Budapest, I could invest in an office building and get a 13 14 15 cap rate. Vienna, an hour away, was five. Same tenants, same construction quality, same credit of your tenant. Well, why was there such a big gap in in return? Well, it was the liquidity. Was the liquidity going to be there someday? And so for me, it was it was a lot of the roll up your sleeves and really it was just a great way to to learn a business, to deal with fragmented markets and so again, very lucky opportunity. >> As you looked at something that was different, you can measure out that difference in cap rate and say, well, there's a return premium if you get your arms around it. How do you know or when do you decide that the work is worth it? Like how much better does it have to be to get excited about it? >> It's a it's a great question. I mean, I think, you know, for me, it was really looking at and and again, when I was doing Central Europe and a lot of it has a lot of it has a lot of similarities to why I'm doing what I'm doing today with Harrison Street in terms of the fragmentation and people dabbling. These were these were assets and and markets where the big European funds would maybe do 5 or 10% investing in in these countries. And I asked where I said, well, why don't I be the pure play guy? I'll be the pure play fund investor just in these markets. I'll do the hard work, roll up roll up the sleeves. But it was that analysis of where was too much risk. Well, okay, when you looked at Ukraine or Russia, okay, they're not part of NATO. What's going to happen to those countries long term? Okay, let's stay away. So really I I synthesized it down to the sort of risk return. Okay, if I invest in these countries that are part of NATO, someday they should become part of the European Union, which would get more institutional interest. But in the meantime, I'll get paid back in five or six years. And so for signing, you know, 10 12 year leases, okay, it's a good risk return analysis. So I kind of looking at it like that. Okay, where is that right level of risk versus return? And again, I couldn't Ukraine, Russia, too much risk. Really, there was no upside that was worth it in my opinion. >> Here's how you thought about your duration of time. So you spot this opportunity to opaque. You're doing all this leg work, but real estate's a pretty long duration asset. So do you say, oh, I'll just spend the rest of my life in Central Europe being the Central Europe real estate person? >> it was interesting. You know, when I went there, it was, you know, I was a transaction guy. I was a deal guy. And so I'd, you know, say, hey, you know, here's a great investment, send the money over, and the money wasn't there. And it wasn't, you know, not not a lot of US pension funds and investors were ready to invest in this market. So it sort of forced me to go develop my own relationships, which was a lot of fun. So I ended up, you know, raising the first funds for Central Europe and did a series of them. And you know, for me, those relationships were were fantastic. It was a lot of fun because it was really inventing the new. And you know, in real estate and you know, a real assets business, you know, such a commodity business, it's hard to differentiate yourself. And so for me, being able to launch the first of something, you know, plenty of people said no, plenty of people said you're crazy. Um but nobody said, you know what, you're the 10th guy that came to my office pitching me that idea. So that's what I've always liked doing. I I again, I I can take the nose. I can take a lot of nose, but I don't want to hear you're just doing what everyone else is doing. And so that is where it started. That's where the light bulb started coming on is, okay, how can you create relevance? How can you create products and ideas that really are first and we really are different because in a way there's less risk to that. And so that was kind of that that was sort of the epiphany for me. >> What was the step from being able to do this inside of Hyman to going and forming Harrison Street? >> So again, very lucky. I I came back to the States after being in Europe for a while. My daughter was born in London. I had got my MBA when I was in London at night. I I I came back. I wanted to come back and be close to the family. Came back to Chicago and you know, continued to travel um and and and managed the business with some some good folks and some good partners. We we had a really really solid team in the region. But I'd love that I loved the building. I loved the creating. I loved the innovation. I had an entrepreneurial bug in me and I said, boy, I'd love to do that again. But number one, what's the idea? Number two, where's the money going to come from? And so for me, it was just so much luck um and and and how it all came together. And so number one the first was the idea. Um what could I do that really I could go add value to investors that somebody else wasn't doing? Uh there was there's plenty of very successful real estate managers out there. This was 2004 2005. So basically it was very similar. I saw that people were dabbling just like in Central Europe, people dabbled and you know, a small part of the bigger funds with Central Europe. People were dabbling in some of the demographic segments. They were dabbling in medical or dabbling in student housing or dabbling in self storage. There wasn't there wasn't a pure play manager that was offering, you want exposure to these, we will be a pure play alts demographic investor. We're not going to try and time cycles. It's all going to be about good fundamentals. So I said, okay, here's a concept. I'm going to I want to launch a business around demographic real estate. Very similar liquidity features as what was happening in Central Europe. It was a small part of the market. A lot of people said you're nuts. You know, student housing is animal house. Senior housing is too operationally intensive. You're not going to get scale in storage. So there was plenty of people that said I couldn't do it. So one that was the idea. And then the second was, okay, now how do you put that in place? Well, I had been a first time fund been had been through the consultant colonoscopies and so I knew, okay, to do this right, have to build a team, have to build your policies and procedures, you know, have to start building a track record. Um and so again in these lucky things in life, a a mentor of mine uh growing up was a guy by the name of Chris Galvin, um who was the chairman and CEO of Motorola. His grandfather, Paul Galvin, founded Motorola. It was a you know, Chicago-based business. Um, and he'd always [clears throat] been a mentor of mine. He's always someone I could go to talk about business, talk about career. thought he'd be with Motorola forever. And I basically was talking about this idea and he he basically said we're I'm leaving Motorola. Um, I'm taking the the the family off um out of this stock. Uh, we're going to set up a family office. I love what you're doing. I loved what you did in Europe. Um, your idea sounds very interesting. There's nowhere for me or my family to invest like that. So why don't we be partners? And he gave me the capital to start and we started a 50/50 partnership and that's where the name Harrison Street comes from. Motorola started on Harrison Street in Chicago. So for me it was very lucky because I got to embark on building a business with a guy who was managing 150,000 employees. And so it was a it was having this organizational development partner that helped me think about culture and people and inventing the new was really cool. And again, I think allowed me to shape and grow this business to where it is today. >> What were some of those early lessons and how did you go about doing that to build the culture, build the organization? >> I think it was just really a a family first, a people first, you know, in environment that, you know, it's not just about it's not just about offering somebody the the most money. Um, it's how do you create alignment of interest? How do you create intellectual uh stimulation for people? How do you give people growth opportunities? Um, how do you create a family environment? How do you create an environment that's not sharp elbows where it's a team? Uh, you're going to go through a lot of ups and downs together. You know, how do you have honesty, humility, uh transparency? Um, and it's sort of, you know, a lot of common sense stuff, but really thinking through and you know, I spend a lot of time on that even today. You know, the the our HR team reports right to me because it's so important and it's a great way we can really differentiate our business because a lot of us are doing very similar things, but if we can do it with the right people. Um, and it 's people that, like I said, have humility and we're all going to make mistakes. Let's raise our hand and let's use those mistakes as almost like a badge of honor as to why people should invest with us because we're taking those and those are, you know, lessons that we learn. But he, you know, he pushed me very much on innovation. He pushed me on, you know, a lot of people thinks people think doing the new is very risky. In a way, you have the space to yourself, so it's less risky. And so Motorola was a business that every decade created an industry that didn't exist a decade before. So it was a very cool way to think about a commodity type business. And they all and he also instilled in me a process. Um, Motorola really uh made Six Sigma really invented his father really created Six Sigma. And Six Sigma quality control was then, you know, Jack Welch made it famous at GE. But you know, thinking about where are the defects in a in a model. Um, and it can be any business you can do. And so for me, it was really thinking about he pushed me where can the mistakes be made. You know, taking recourse, you know, taking too much leverage, uh trying to time markets by, you know, markets that are just economic cycles. Um, and so it kind of kept pushing me to say where can the mistakes are there, where the mistakes are there. So trying to think about the mistakes ahead of time so you can build that into your process. So it was just a different way of thinking which was really cool and again really lucky for me to be part of. >> One of the challenges in asset management when you're trying to do something innovative is if you're the only one doing it, you get a lot of skeptics. What was it like when you first went out with this idea into the marketplace? >> You know, it's funny. So we, you know, I remember going out with our first fund and, you know, no one had tried to do um you know, uh 100% only fund around education, healthcare, and storage. And I remember, you know, I dragged Chris to to a meeting with actually we went to a uh a meeting at an endowment's office. And, [clears throat] you know, they said the whole time you can't do this. You're not going to be able to work with multiple partners. You know, student housing is animal house. There's not going to be liquidity in these sectors. Yeah, we haven't seen this before. You know, we'd rather try and do it ourselves. We out of the meeting and and and and and you know, look, I had left a career. You know, I didn't have a lot of money and you know, I just had I think my wife was pregnant with our third kid. I just had my first house. So it was, you know, [laughter] it was pretty pretty nervous. And you know, I walk out of this meeting pretty dejected. And Chris looks at me and says, that's the best meeting you're ever going to go to. And I said I said, what are you talking about? He said, when experts tell you you can't do something, you know you're onto something. And he said, that's exactly when you know you have something is when the people that are supposed to be the experts tell you you can't do something, then you've got something. And it was pretty an interesting way to look at it. And I I don't know if I necessarily believed him at the time, but you know, I think that was the you know, that was the was interesting. It was, you know, going and talking to folks and hearing a lot of people say no, uh but at the same time, then there was a lot of folks that said, no, this is that's pretty interesting what you're doing. We saw what you did in Central Europe. You saw how that you know, cuz I was very lucky. Those markets ended up developing and cap rates compressed and the investors did very well there and a lot of people said, no, this makes a lot of sense what you're doing. And then what really what really, I think helped the business was two years into it, we hit the global financial crisis. And very tough time to start a business, especially a real estate business. Um but in a way it it it it it shined a light on, wait a second. Our medical office properties did better than office. Our student senior did better than multi. Our stores are better than industrial. These were need-based assets. People go to school and go in bad times. They get old and so all of a sudden people said, well, maybe you're onto something. And that kind of helped us keep pushing forward with new ideas. >> This original idea of demographic-based investing or finding those opportunities, what does that mean when you bring it into practice to get to student housing or senior living? >> I think it was it was where could I add value in the system? When what Chris kept pushing me on is where can where are people making mistakes in real estate? Obviously the big mistake in real estate is trying to time markets, trying to time cycles. Leverage. And so it pushed me to, well, demographics, it's not trying to time cycles, right? If you are looking at education and healthcare, if you're looking for need-based assets where it's not necessarily pricing, it's it's more social infrastructure. Okay, these are asset classes that have good long-term fundamentals. My entry point isn't as important. At the same time, the reason that a lot of capital wasn't going to these sectors was fragmentation, hard to access. So perfect, you know, perfect for a young team to let's roll up our sleeves and let's go access it, let's do the hard work. And again, you know, the first fund we raised I think was 200 million. I had no idea where this would evolve into. But for me, it was I could add value to my investors. I could sit across the table and say, look at you're a big pension fund, you're a big insurance company, you're not going to go screw around with doing a five or 10 million dollar deal. I can go do the hard work. I will build the infrastructure to do the hard work to, again, the thesis was we're going to go do a lot of one-off investments, but our liquidity is going to come from selling big portfolios. And again, at the time we, you know, there was a lot of people that I guess sort of bet on us, but when I look back today, probably 80 80 to 90% of our investments are still individual investments, but 80 to 90% of our sales are through big portfolios. So it's it's really come to fruition. >> So if you look at some of these areas, when you first started looking at say student housing with the premise that this might be Animal House, what [snorts] work did you do that other people weren't doing to go in and get comfortable that it's a great opportunity? >> You know, I wouldn't say others weren't doing it. People people maybe were dabbling a little bit, but the work we did was let's go spend time at these schools. Let's go see what sort of housing there is because again, the amount of deferred maintenance on these campuses. Um, the big public universities just don't have the capital for off-campus housing. People were living in, you know, just um, I'd say older um, not great houses. Um, but there was an industry that was developing where there was building these purpose-built, you know, almost like multi-family but for students. And it was a a new and up-and-coming area and I had met a number of these developers and they took me on tours and we looked at properties and it was basically just, you know, multi-family product for students, you know, bed bath parity and really renting by the room versus by the unit. Uh, parent guarantees. And so really went and spent time and and then started really digging into some of the issues where, okay, these kids are going to destroy it. No, actually they're not because we walk the units and if there's a hole in the wall, we send the bill to the parents and if they do it again, we kick them out. And so if you treat them like adults, actually they take good care of the property. Uh, larger percentage of it were women than men. Um, well, what about insurance costs? Oh my god, they must be off the charts. Actually not because, you know, what's interesting about insurance is the number one, in fact the insurance costs for multi-family are more than student housing. Number one cause of insurance claims in in in student housing or in in multi-family um, is kitchen fires. And the kids don't use the kitchens. So there's a lot of things when you peel back the onion and do your work, you can recognize, okay, this isn't. And you know what? We do believe this will develop into an institutional market at some point. But that was that was the thesis and that was what was interesting for me, it was very similar to Central Europe because was there going to be an institutional market developing? And this to me was, okay, we can invest, get good prices. You know, kids are going to the University of Michigan, University of Texas, ASU, they're going to go to school in good and bad times. And, you know, we've got good consistent occupancy, we're getting good returns on our investment. Okay, we think this is good solid investing. Let's see what happens. >> As you built that out over the years, what did you learn about what types of schools make sense to go improve own property? >> Well, and and that's been our secret >> Now we've done 1,300 of these and 80 billion across these sectors. So we've really learned what works and doesn't. You know, we've made plenty of mistakes. And to me, it's it's it's it's the right school you need to be at. Um you need to be in the right location at that campus. You need to have the right unit mix. And then you need the right local operating partner that knows knows really how to lease to students. Um you know, roommate matching. Um people are moving in and out within a two-week period of time. So how do you work with your vendors to do that? So there's a lot of nuances to operating these assets that you need the right partners. And we've been so fortunate to be doing this for two decades. We've got some great partners um that you know, almost become family in a way. Um we've had some bad partners. Um but I think for us it's we've created almost like a scoring model now of what does a school need to have? What does that market need to look like? Because there are enrollment takers and then there's probably 15 to 20% of schools will go out of business. And so the mistakes that people are going to make now coming into these industries is thinking, okay, all student housing is the same, which isn't the case. Um and so again, there's a lot that goes into, okay, why this school? Why now? Uh there's a lot of interest in the sector. So again, for us it's always kind of trying to stay true to, here's the model, here's the mistakes we made, let's not make them again. But then we've also tried to create diversified funds. We don't want all the capital to have to go into student or go into senior. And we're seeing a lot of people do that. And that's where you can make mistakes. If you just have to push all the capital into one asset class, well, if that asset class is not the right risk return in that given year, we don't want to participate. So we've tried to build these more diversified strategies. So okay, if senior housing is a good risk return, let's let's focus more there this year. >> What have you built up on the team and the resources, the knowledge over the years, let's just say in that student housing vertical compared to you know, when you were just doing it one off? >> Yeah, I mean I think you know, our team has really become domain experts now. We don't do property management leasing but we've got project management, we've got construction management, got a great asset management team, we've got a great investment team. The the expertise is there so we're a great capital to partner to developers and operators because we know the business. We actually bring them opportunities. But it's morphed into even more. We we now are not only we the largest sort of off-campus owner of of of student housing and senior housing but you know now we're probably the largest owner of on campus. We'll work with their district energy, their wastewater. Basically saying let let us help you with this problem you have with capital. And that's what's been fun for us is kind of just deepening the relationships with these partners like health systems, like universities. >> On the other end of the demographic spectrum we have the senior housing which you mentioned a couple times. What did that progression look like? >> Very similar. I think very similar. Um you know it's it's a business that you have to be a a bit more patient. Um I think we've we really have developed great relationships with great operators. Uh it's a very local regional business. These are these are groups that what I love is these are people most of our partners started the business by creating senior product because they wanted to take care of their parents or their mom. And so there's a love for the business, there's a passion for the business, the restaurant's named after their mother. Um but we now have great you know great partners in the Northwest, great partners in Long Island, great partners you know on the East Coast. And so the progression was the same. Just very patient. Let's focus on it. Let's you know, we made some mistakes early on, and we sort of now figured out what the secret sauce is for the right product, you know, independent assisted memory care, private pay, the right agent income qualified markets. So again, I think cutting our teeth over the past 20 years, we've kind of figured out, okay, this is the right unit mix, this is the right market location, this is the right affordability numbers we need to look at. And so again, just those cycles of learning and just, you know, again, being honest about, hey, we made mistakes and here's what we're doing. And and that's always a frustration for me. You know, there's not enough humility. I mean, you know, to me, the mistakes we made, what I tell our team, those are the reasons that people should want to invest with us now going forward. There's all these new people coming into these sectors. Well, they're going to make mistakes. There's no doubt about it. I've made those mistakes and I built that into my model now. So why shouldn't that be something we should yell from the rooftops? Here's the list of mistakes we made. We don't do it again. And this is why. And so at any event, I think for us, the progression, whether it's senior housing, whether it's in medical office, whether it's in self-storage, whether it's in our infrastructure business, it's it's just let's find good relationships. Let's be patient, one deal at a time, but stay true to our our thesis of how we manage and think about risk, you know. We don't take recourse risk. We don't take cost overruns. So it's really trying to stay true to a lot of the tenants that got us here as we grow the business. >> What are some of the examples of those mistakes that most stick with you? >> I I you you the podcast is probably not long enough for me to tell them all, but you know, you know, I think, you know, we've certainly learned about whether certain offtakes, whether it's, you know, what universities you want to be part of. We've certainly learned mistakes about banking relationships. You know, we dealt with some banks that were taken over by the FDIC and you know, the GFC probably wouldn't have even thought we've got underwrite our our banking relationships that much. Um, we've learned a lot about the level of care at senior housing, memory care only versus having the continuum of care. Um, so you know, it's really there's a lot we've learned, you know, what the right unit count is for student housing. A lot of people are doing very large student housing assets that are 1,200 1,500. We think those are very too big. Um, so there's a sweet spot in terms of what the right number is to manage, uh, the right unit mix. You want bed bath parity, you don't want to be too far from campus in most cases. So basically every asset class we have a list of a dozen or so lessons that we've learned. Um, and again we use that in our investment process now to say, okay, let's make sure we don't do that again. >> On senior living, there's a big kind of service [clears throat] and care component to it that won't exist in student housing or self storage. I mean, we're doing a lot of stuff in student that has to do with behavioral health and wellness and things like that. So we're trying to to do that because how can we make our project how can we differentiate the customer experience, right? So I think even in storage, how can we make the customer experience different? Because you're going through life events, divorces, deaths, marriage, like there's things happening. So how can you make that customer experience much better? So all these asset classes you can do that in a way. Um, so I think with senior housing, you know, what you learn is you have to really understand number one food service. I mean, you've got a pretty discerning audience, right? They're eating two to three times a day at the same restaurant. So you better have a really understanding of food service. How are you doing how are you taking care of health needs? Are you outsourcing it or are you insourcing it? How are you thinking of the evolution, the continuum of care, you know, whether it's a couple and one starts to have levels of dementia and the other one doesn't?
